docs.checked.title: Checked by the test suite
docs.checked.body: Every code block in the guide is parsed, checked and type-checked on each release.
hero.title: One language for the web, and the page it prints to.
hero.sub: WebFluent is a typed language that compiles to a static site, a single-page app, a PDF or a slide deck. It is one binary: no Node, no bundler, no config — and a compiler that finds your mistakes before a browser does.
hero.nodeps: No Node, no bundler, no config
hero.watch: watching src/ — the page reloads on save
video.title: Rethinking the web layout
ideas.title: Five ideas, and the rest follows
idea.1.title: A file is declarations
idea.1.body: Thirteen kinds — `page`, `component`, `store`, `theme`, `app`, `type`, `enum`, `api`, `const`, `data`, `image`, `animation` and `test`. Each page names its own route; there is no route table to keep in sync.
idea.2.title: An element is a typed call
idea.2.body: One positional value, named props, flags after a dot, then a block. The compiler knows what every built-in and every component of yours accepts.
idea.3.title: State is a signal
idea.3.body: `state count = 0`, and whatever reads it follows it. Derived values recompute and only the text or attribute that changed updates. No dependency arrays.
idea.4.title: Styles are CSS, beside the element
idea.4.body: A `style { }` block is real CSS — values, `$tokens` from your theme, `&:hover` and media queries — compiled to one stylesheet with only what you used.
idea.5.title: The build is the whole site
idea.5.body: `wf build` writes pre-rendered HTML for each page, a runtime cut to what you use, a sitemap, link previews and a content-security policy the build checks itself against.
ideas.react.title: Coming from React, Vue or Svelte?
ideas.react.body: Start from what you know: state is a signal, components are declared and typed, stores replace context, and `resource` replaces your data-fetching library.
outputs.title: One source, four things to ship
outputs.lede: `build.output_type` in `webfluent.app.json` chooses what `wf build` writes. The PDF and slides come from the compiler's own layout engine — no headless browser.
output.spa.title: Single-page app
output.spa.body: One shell and a router that draws pages in the browser, each page's code fetched the first time its route shows.
output.static.title: Static site
output.static.body: One pre-rendered HTML file per route that works before any script loads, then hydrates in place. The right default for anything people search for.
output.pdf.title: PDF document
output.pdf.body: Invoices, reports and résumés, laid out with the same CSS as the web: headers, footers, page breaks, charts and Arabic text.
output.slides.title: Slide deck
output.slides.body: A `Presentation` of `Slide`s written like any other page, one slide per PDF page — generated from your data if you like.
cta.title: Build your first page
cta.body: The tutorial takes you from an empty folder to a deployed site in about half an hour — data, components, a store, a form, a theme and a test along the way.
footer.built: Every code block in the guide is real WebFluent {version}, parsed, type-checked and compiled by the test suite.
notfound.title: Nothing lives here
notfound.body: The address you followed does not match any page. The guide's first chapter is a good place to start again.
search.label: Search the guide
ref.intro: {count} built-in elements in eleven groups, each with its signature, its props, its flags, its events and its parts — read from the compiler's registry, so what this page lists is exactly what the checker accepts. Every element is written `Name(positional, prop: value).flag { block }`.
ref.noprops: This element takes no props of its own.
ref.attrs: Attribute families: `{families}`. Plus the {n} universal props every element takes: {props}.
ref.domevents: The DOM events it is drawn to answer. Any other DOM event works too, in an `on … { }` handler.
ref.flags.body: A flag is written after the parentheses with a dot: a `Bool` prop, or a case of one of the element's enum props. A case the enum lacks is an error with a hint.
ref.events.body: Every element accepts these in an `on … { }` handler; an element's own events come first.
ref.generated.title: Generated, not written
ref.generated.body: This page comes from the compiler's registry. Edit the registry, not the page — a prop added there shows up here on the next release.
ref.universal.title: On every element
ref.universal.body: Every element takes these props, and the HTML attribute families named on it (`aria-*`, `data-*`, and the global attributes such as `id`, `class`, `title`, `role`, `tabindex`).
ref.icons.body: The names Icon(…), IconButton(icon:) and Sidebar.Item(icon:) draw; any other name shows as the word, and the compiler warns.
ref.renders: Renders with the class `{cls}`, stable across releases, so a stylesheet may target it.
batteries.title: What a real site needs, already in the language
bat.api.title: A service, described once
bat.api.body: `api Backend { get users() -> [User] }` — every call typed, cached, retried and cancellable. Or read the whole service from an OpenAPI file.
bat.forms.title: Forms that validate themselves
bat.forms.body: `validate email { required  email }` beside the state. The field shows its message accessibly, and a failed submit moves focus to the problem.
bat.realtime.title: Sockets, streams and peers
bat.realtime.body: WebSockets that reconnect, server-sent events, a channel every tab hears and WebRTC to another reader's page — each closed when its page leaves.
bat.offline.title: Works offline
bat.offline.body: Name `offline` in the config: a service worker stores the site, writes wait for the connection, and a new version is offered, never forced.
bat.tests.title: Tests that click
bat.tests.body: `click "Save"` then `expect "Saved"` runs in a real browser, and `wf verify` loads every page of the build and fails on any error.
bat.security.title: Safe by construction
bat.security.body: Text is always text, there are no inline handlers or `javascript:` links, private `env` values stay out of the bundle, and the build holds itself to a strict CSP.
bat.js.title: Your JavaScript, by name
bat.js.body: A plain `.js` file under `src/` is linked as written, and its functions are called straight from `.wf`, checked against their JSDoc.
consent.label: Cookie consent
consent.title: Analytics
consent.body: This site uses Google Analytics to count visits. It sets cookies only if you allow it; you can change your mind under Cookie settings at the bottom of any page.
showcase.title: Showcase
showcase.lede: Real files from real source. Each one is what `wf build` wrote from a folder under `examples/`, and every release builds it again — so what you see is what this version makes.
showcase.more: Each one is a folder under [`examples/`](https://github.com/monzeromer-lab/WebFluent/tree/master/examples) that builds with `wf build`. [PDF and slides](/docs/guide/pdf-and-slides) in the guide says how to write your own.
outputs.see: See the PDFs and decks it writes
start.title: A running site in three commands
start.body: Install `wf`, create a project from a template, and start the dev server. There is nothing else to install and nothing to configure first.
start.steps:
1. `wf init` writes a small, working project — pages, components, a store and tests — so you start from something real.
2. `wf serve` builds it and serves it. Open `http://localhost:3000`.
3. Edit `src/pages/Home.wf` and save: the page rebuilds and reloads. A mistake shows over the page, with its fix, until you save again.
check.title: Mistakes are errors, not blank pages
check.body: Every element, prop, flag, record field and store member has a declared shape, and the compiler holds your program to it. A typo is caught where you wrote it, with the fix — not discovered later as something missing in the browser.
check.point1: Types, accessibility, search and security checked on every build
check.point2: The same findings in your editor, as you type
check.point3: wf explain T05 prints any code's full explanation
studio.title: An app made for writing WebFluent
studio.body: A code editor, a live preview, a visual designer, Git and this guide in one window, with the compiler running inside it. There is no terminal and no dev server, and a project built in Studio is byte-identical to `wf build`.
studio.point1: Each error comes with the compiler's fix, one click away
studio.point2: Design mode writes the `.wf` you would have written
studio.point3: An agent whose changes you accept hunk by hunk
studio.note: Version 0.1 for Linux, macOS and Windows, with Android to follow. Studio is a separate, closed-source app; `wf` and any editor are all you need.
studio.alt: WebFluent Studio in Design mode: the layers on the left, the page on the canvas with the site's navigation selected, and the inspector on the right
bat.i18n.title: Every language, both directions
bat.i18n.body: One JSON file per locale and `t("key")` to read it. Plurals follow each language's rules, and Arabic or Hebrew flips the page right to left.
